WHO is not liable for any damages arising from the use of its materials. An After Action Review (AAR) is a qualitative evaluation of actions taken during an emergency response. It identifies best practices, gaps, lessons learned, and challenges encountered. AARs are structured to assess what worked well, how these practices can be institutionalized, and what did not work, requiring corrective action. They are essential for fostering a culture of continuous learning and improvement. AARs are not external evaluations of individual or team performance. Instead, they provide a constructive, collective learning opportunity for stakeholders involved in public health preparedness and response. AARs can range from informal debriefing sessions to larger workshops with multisectoral participation. They rely on open, honest, and equal interaction among participants and follow a consistent analytical framework to understand what should have happened, what actually happened, what went well, what did not, and how improvements can be made. The WHO recommends AARs as part of the International Health Regulations (IHR) Monitoring and Evaluation Framework (MEF) to assess the functionality of core capacities and contribute to the development of comprehensive national action plans for health security. AARs are typically quick, facilitated, safe, flexible, and time-bound processes conducted shortly after an event. They are pedagogical and interactive, often combining data collection with facilitated workshops involving response participants. The outcomes of AARs should be actionable, producing recommendations for decision-makers and contributing to national planning cycles. WHO has developed guidance and toolkits for conducting AARs, including templates, checklists, facilitators' manuals, and trigger questions. These tools standardize and simplify the AAR process, ensuring that lessons learned are documented and accessible through a lessons learned database. This database builds institutional memory and serves as a resource for emergency preparedness and response stakeholders. The WHO guidance for AARs, published in 2019, outlines the entire process, from planning and conducting an AAR to reporting findings and following up on proposed actions. The guidance emphasizes the importance of creating a repository of key challenges, best practices, and recommendations to ensure that lessons are not lost and can inform future responses.
